text: Quod mihi cum Francisco Turriano, viro alioqui erudito probeque in Græcis versato, sequentia qui opuscula Ingolstadii anno 1615 Latine solum edidit, in his Maximi opusculis non ubique convĕnit, eorumque novam ipse adornavi versionem, cum Græco ipso textu ex probatissimis codd. arcessito, producendam (id est, ex rev. Gerasimi Blacchi codice, ex meliori viri et Raph. Dufresnii emendato,) operæ pretium putavi paucula adnotare, quibus et lucis aliquid forte auctori afferam, et mei consilii rationem, ejus judicium omne permittendo lectori, aperiam, uti fere primo sextoque tom. Operum Chrysostomi factitatum Ducæo.
en: What I have in common with Franciscus Turrianus, an erudite man and well versed in Greek, who published the following opuscula in Latin only at Ingolstadt in 1615, is that in these opuscula of Maximus he does not agree everywhere; and I have prepared my own new version of them, to be issued with the Greek text itself drawn from the best manuscripts (that is, from the codex of Rev. Gerasimus Blachus, emended from the better one of Raphael Dufresne). I thought it worth the effort to add a few notes, by which I may perhaps bring some light to the author and open up the reason for my plan, leaving the whole judgment to the reader, as I mostly did in the first and sixth volumes of the works of Chrysostom, in Ducaeus's manner.

text: Τὴν τῶν ὄντων φύσιν περιγράφων. Vis hujus vocis hic est, obliterans, e numero auferens, ac circumscribens; quo sensu etiam Cicero eam usurpavit vocem; nec aliud est quod sequitur περιορίζων. Uti enim ad virtutem superanda natura, ita etiam ad scientiam omnino certam motus omnis temporis ac ævi: quo spectet illud Hesych. Περιοριστόν, περίγραπτον: nec apte Turr. terminans ac definiens. Τὸ ἐνώσεως: plane mendum est, pro γνώσεως: cui uni etiam congruit epithetum ἀπλανοῦς. et quæ contra ἀρετὴν ubique Maximo aliisque distinguitur; scientia scilicet, non unitio vel conjunctio. Optime Schol. Maximi mentem aperit.
anchorLine: ἀρετῆς γένεσιν τὴν τῶν ὄντων φύσιν περιγράφων (a)
en: The sense of this word is: obliterating, removing from the number, and circumscribing; Cicero also used the word in this sense; and what follows, περιορίζων, is no different. For as nature is to be surpassed for virtue, so also for entirely certain knowledge, the motion of all time and age; compare Hesychius: Περιοριστόν, περίγραπτον. Turrianus's 'terminating and defining' is not apt. The word ἐνώσεως is plainly a mistake for γνώσεως, to which alone the epithet ἀπλανοῦς (unerring) is also fitting, and which is everywhere distinguished by Maximus and others from virtue (ἀρετή); that is, knowledge, not union or conjunction. The Scholiast best reveals Maximus's meaning.

text: Τοῦ δὲ βίου φύσις. Turrianus: Ratio vero persona vitæ; sive ita habuit ejus cod. sive scribenti obrepsit, loco φύσις, πρόσωπον, manifesto circulo, quem et repræsentat dum in margine ita observat: Ratio sustentatur vita, et vita ratione; s[?]. est ratio hypostasis sive persona vitæ, et vita rationis. Frigida hæc, nec ex Maximi mente, quam Schol. Dufrenii cod. recte aperit; ipseque conatus sum reddere. Rationis vita persona exstitit, qua scilicet repræsentetur et conspicua fiat, uti alibi ipse Maximus; vel etiam ei basis exsistat: vita autem natura seu essentia, ratio, quæ vim omnem vitæ tribuat, id est, virtuti; sitque illi fere, id quod anima corpori.
anchorLine: (on p-0011) σοι γέγονε πρόσωπον (2) ὁ βίος· τοῦ δὲ βίου φύ-
en: 'Of life, the nature.' Turrianus has: 'Reason, but the person of life', whether his codex read so or it slipped in on the writer, with πρόσωπον in place of φύσις, plainly by a circle, which he also reproduces when he notes in the margin: 'Reason is sustained by life, and life by reason'; that is, reason is the hypostasis or person of life, and life of reason. This is cold and not from Maximus's mind, which the Scholiast of Dufresne's codex rightly discloses; and I have myself tried to render it. Life became the person of reason, by which it is represented and made conspicuous, as Maximus himself says elsewhere; or it may even be its base: life, however, is nature or essence, reason that which assigns all force to life, that is, to virtue; and it is to it roughly what the soul is to the body.

text: Ὄρεξις φανταστικὴ τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν καὶ οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Sensus integer est, nec aliud habent Dufrenii cod. et Venet. in quo etiam, vel certe ejus typographo, deest τὸ, καὶ οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν· non levi mendo: quo tamen ipso ad explendam lacunam ex Turriani codice proclive utor. Explicavit illo Maximus, quid sit τὸ φανταστικόν· esse nimirum τὸ διανοητικόν, vim scilicet cogitandi, ad quam sequitur et cui comes appetitio eorum quæ in nostra sunt facultate, et quæ in ea minime posita sunt; absque scilicet deliberatione rationis, quæ est solum τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν, eorum quæ nostræ sunt facultatis: nec bene additur in Turriano, et quæ non sunt. Stultum enim est deliberare de his quæ non sunt in nostra facultate: non autem simplici appetitu ex phantasia ac cogitando ea velle, motu potius brutis affine, quam ex ratione. Lacunæ occasio fuit repetitio τοῦ, τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν, quo nihil proclivius, ut aliquid omittatur.
anchorLine: οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν (c) · τουτέστι μόνῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ μορφου-
en: The reading 'Appetite that is imaginative of what is up to us and not up to us': the sense is whole; Dufresne's codex and the Venetian have nothing else, in which (or at least in its printer's copy) the phrase 'and not up to us' is missing, by no slight fault; to fill the gap I readily use Turrianus's codex. Maximus there explains what the imaginative faculty (phantastikon) is: namely the intellectual (dianoetikon), the power of thinking, upon which follows, as companion, the appetite for things that are in our power and for things not at all in it, without the deliberation of reason, which belongs only to what is up to us. Turrianus does not do well to add 'and what are not'; for it would be foolish to deliberate about things that are not in our power, and not by simple appetite to wish them by imagining and thinking, a motion more akin to brutes than from reason. The occasion of the gap was the repetition of 'τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν', than which nothing is easier, so that something is omitted.

text: Οὐ πᾶσιν. Hæc ex Nem. cap. 33, totidem vocibus; in quibus aliquid forte luxatum, ut quadrent cum inductione quæ sequitur, eorum, quæ a nobis appeti voluntate possint, sed non eligi, quod non sint nostræ facultatis, nec habeant rationem medii, sed finis. Esset ergo dicendum: Non omnibus quibus convenit voluntate appeti, omnino etiam convenit eligi: nisi excidit vox, καὶ τὸ ἔμπαλιν, vicissimque; ad quam spectet illa inductio.
anchorLine: Οὐ πᾶσιν (d) οἷς ἁρμόζει τὸ προαιρεῖσθαι, πάντως
en: 'Not for all.' This is from Nemesius, chapter 33, in the same words; in which something is perhaps dislocated, so that they fit the induction that follows, of things that can be desired by will but not chosen, because they are not within our power and do not have the character of a means but of an end. So one should say: 'Not for all to whom it belongs to be desired by will does it also belong to be chosen', unless the phrase 'and conversely' has dropped out, to which that induction would refer.

text: Περὶ φρονήματος. Etiam Cicero laborat reddenda hac voce. Aliis cogitatum, sensus, prudentia, intelligentia, sapientia; sic enim etiam φρονεῖν, sapere: quandoque etiam animus et appetitus. Quam hic Maximus harum vocum proprietatem observat, auctores liberiore earum usu fere negligunt. Quod definit Maximus, φρόνησιν, id est prudentiam, ἕξιν ἀνοίας καὶ ὑπερνοίας ἀντίπαλον: non bene reddit Turr. sive ejus cod. habuit ἀγνοίας, sive fefellit oculus, aut mens præcurrit, Ignorantiæ adversariam, imo, mentis inopiæ, dementiæ, imprudentiæ per defectum; uti ὑπερνοίας, per excessum, quam sufficientiam, dicere possimus; vitium scilicet ὑψινοίᾳ affine, id est superbiæ; qua quis eximie et supra reliquos putat se sapere.
anchorLine: Περὶ φρονήματος (e), ἤγουν φρονήσεως.
en: On φρόνημα (mindset). Cicero too has trouble rendering this word. Others render it: thought, sense, prudence, intelligence, wisdom; so also φρονεῖν, to be wise; sometimes also mind and appetite. How carefully Maximus observes the proper sense of these words, while authors almost neglect them in their freer usage. Maximus defines φρόνησις, that is prudence, as 'a state opposed to folly and to over-wisdom': Turrianus (or his codex, which had ἀγνοίας; or his eye failed, or his mind ran ahead) does not render it well as 'opposed to ignorance'; rather, 'to poverty of mind, madness, imprudence by defect', as ὑπερνοία (over-wisdom), by excess, we may call self-sufficiency; a vice akin to ὑψινοία, that is, pride, by which one thinks oneself exceptionally wise and above the rest.

text: Καὶ ἄδηλον ἐχόντων τὸ τέλος· Sic Dufrenii cod. pro quo errore Venet. Εὔδηλον· quod etiam habuit Turriani, dum reddit, et certum finem habent; imo certe incertum: sic enim ipse Maximus, Περὶ ὧν βουλευόμεθα· De quibus deliberamus (quæ ipsa sunt circa quæ electio versatur) non satis esse ait, ut in nostra sint facultate, et per nos fiant; sed necessario addendum, καὶ ἄδηλον ἐχόντων τὸ τέλος· et incertum habent finem: cujus debuit vir doctus non sic facile oblivisci; cum præcipue res sic plana sit, et sic habeat Nem. textus, quem Maximus sublegit.
anchorLine: των τὸ τέλος (f) ἐστίν· ἐφ' ἡμῖν δὲ, καὶ ὁ τῶν ἀρε-
en: 'And having an uncertain end.' So Dufresne's codex; for which the Venetian has, by error, Εὔδηλον ('quite clear'), which Turrianus also had when he rendered 'and have a certain end'; rather, certainly 'uncertain': for Maximus himself says in 'On what we deliberate' (the very things about which choice is exercised) that it is not enough that they be in our power and come about through us, but one must necessarily add 'and having an uncertain end'. The learned man ought not so easily to have forgotten this, especially as the matter is so plain and Nemesius's text has it, which Maximus follows.

text: Τῆς τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὀρεκτοῦ. Venet. ὀρεκτικοῦ, habuitque Turr. cod. plane mendose, nec ipse ullum commodum sensum elicere potuit. Nempe, qui per naturam ὀρεκτικοί sunt (appetendi facultate prædití) ejus nanciscentur mysticam fruitionem seu possessionem, qui per naturam τὸ ὀρεκτὸν est (ipsum natura appetibile) Dei scilicet.
anchorLine: μόνης ἀφράστως ἐπειλημμένη τῆς τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὀρεκτοῦ (g) μυστικῆς ἀπολαύσεως
en: 'Of that which is by nature object of desire.' The Venetian has ὀρεκτικοῦ ('of the desiring'), and Turrianus's codex had it too, quite wrongly, nor could he himself draw out any fitting sense. For those who are by nature desiring (endowed with the faculty of desire) will attain the mystical enjoyment or possession of that which is by nature the desirable (that which is itself desirable by nature), namely God.

text: Ὁ κατὰ φύσιν ὑφίσταται λόγος. Huic opponit quod vitii est, παρυφίσταται quasi umbra quadam ac simulacro exsistit. Id enim mali est, quod non tam ens sit, quam ab eo defectus. Sic Basil. in Hexaem. Οἱονεὶ ἀποσκίασμα τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ ὄντα, αὐτομάτως παρυφίσταται: de illis qui mundum ab æterno ac illi coæternum ponebant. Sic et passim Dionys. Proprie itaque ac delectu verborum locutus est Maximus, etsi Turrianus una voce, nec satis expressa, utraque involvit. Evadit ratio, aut modus.
anchorLine: τῆς εὐχρηστίας ὑφίσταται λόγος (h), ἢ ὁ παρὰ φύσιν
en: 'The reason according to nature subsists.' To this he opposes what belongs to vice, παρυφίσταται (exists alongside), exists as a kind of shadow and semblance. For that is the character of evil, that it is not so much a being as a falling away from it. So Basil in the Hexaemeron: 'as a shadow of its power, existing of itself it comes to subsist alongside': said of those who posited the world from eternity and coeternal with it. So too Dionysius frequently. Maximus therefore spoke properly and with a choice of words, although Turrianus wraps both in one word, not sufficiently expressed. It comes out as 'reason' or 'manner'.

text: cati reatu, exque Adæ prævaricatione universo humano generi invectas; quas Maximus illa quæst. 24, alterum peccatum, quod Christus factus est, Paulina phrasi, exponit: nempe τὸ παθητὸν naturæ, citra omnem culpæ reatum, quo et nobis incorruptionem ac immortalitatem paravit ἀδιάβλητα πάθη vocat Damasc., et alii, quibus sponte factum obnoxium Christum fides docet. Non bene Turr. vir alioqui doctus, passiones nostræ honestatis; nec ipse ubique libratissimas viri θεολογικωτάτου voces, qualis est Maximus, assecutus. Τὰ ἐπιτίμια, vox vel tironibus, in re præsertim ecclesiastica, notissima. Sic passim Græci pœnas omnes ecclesiasticas vocitant, ac quas nos dicimus censuras, scita paranomasia in vocibus, τὰ τῆς ἐπιτιμίας, καὶ τὰ τῆς ἀτιμίας: quæ sunt Latinis, pœna et culpa. Primum certe Christus assumpsit, eoque alterum (quod et sibi arrogavit) sanavit, eaque natura sustulit; quomodo nobis τῆς ἑπομένης φυσικῆς ἀφθαρσίας ἀρραβῶνα δεδώρηται, donavit arrhabonem incorruptionis quæ sequitur ac comes est illis in Christo pœnis: quæ ipsa naturæ innovatio est, sic Maximo, Nysseno, Damasceno, aliisque Patribus Græcis celebrata; naturæ scilicet rectitudo, qualis in Adamo condita est, ipsa in Christo præcedens, ut in capite, ac futura in nobis, ut ejus membris; cujus et nobis in eo arrhabo est. Nec bene Turr. fecit munere suo esse pignus naturalis immortalitatis; quam Christus non assumpsit, sed contrarium, τὸ παθητὸν carnis, ejus vim patiendi ac moriendi; ex Adamo scilicet reo unum hoc mutuatus, ad ejus alterum in nobis reparandum; priorem scilicet ipsius rectitudinem, quæ est illa ejus incorruptio naturalis; summa nempe immunitas ab omni eo quod ex peccato nobis inolevit.
anchorLine: (anchor on p-0021: τῆς ἡμῶν ἐπιτιμίας (i) δι' αὐτῆς τῆς πείρας)
en: ... of the guilt of sin, and brought upon the whole human race from Adam's transgression; which Maximus, in that question 24, explains as 'the other sin', which Christ was made, in Pauline phrase: namely the passible element (to pathēton) of nature, free of any guilt, by which he also procured incorruption and immortality for us; Damascene and others call them 'blameless passions', from which the faith teaches that Christ was voluntarily liable. Turrianus, otherwise learned, does not do well with 'passions of our honesty'; nor has he everywhere grasped the finely balanced words of so theological a man as Maximus. The word ἐπιτίμια is known even to beginners, especially in ecclesiastical matters. So the Greeks commonly call all ecclesiastical penalties, what we call censures, with a clever play on words: 'what belongs to penalty' and 'what belongs to dishonour', which in Latin are 'penalty and guilt'. Christ first assumed the one, and by it healed the other (which he also claimed as his own), and removed the nature of it; whereby he has given us a pledge of the following natural incorruption, he has given a pledge of the incorruption that follows and accompanies those penalties in Christ: which is the very renewal of nature, thus celebrated by Maximus, Nyssen, Damascene and other Greek Fathers; namely the rectitude of nature, as it was established in Adam, going first in Christ as in the head, and to come in us as in his members; of which we too have the pledge in him. Nor did Turrianus do well to make it, by his office, a pledge of natural immortality; which Christ did not assume, but its contrary, the passible element of the flesh, its power of suffering and dying; borrowed from guilty Adam for this one thing, to repair in us his other, namely his original rectitude, which is his natural incorruption; the supreme immunity from everything that has grown in us from sin.

text: Προσεπήγαγον. Non bene Turr. in tertia persona, solius Dei esse adjunxerunt. Ipse enim Maximus est, qui pro se ibi excusat; uti etiam aliis locis, quibus alio modo favere novæ doctrinæ visus sit. Hic clare aperit, quomodo unam solius Dei in beatis operationem, deificationem dixerit; quod nempe actio illa quæ est beatitudo (Dei scilicet visio ac fruitio), ex Deo sit in nobis operante supra totam naturæ ordinem; etsi vere ipsi operemur et vitaliter, at non quasi ipsi nobis actionis principium ac auctores; sed quasi Deo trahente ad id quod divinum est: quo ipso modo dixerit Maximus, non esse illam δικαίων ἔργων τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀντίδοσιν, quod omnino excedat operum merita, quæ ipsa in nobis Dei sint munera, ut loquitur Augustinus. Sed de his theologi.
anchorLine: (not read directly; Greek column, line near '... ἐστιν (7), ἡ κατὰ χάριν τῶν ἁγίων ἐκθέωσις' region, from page thumbnail only)
en: 'They added.' Turrianus does not do well with 'in the third person, they added that it is of God alone'. For Maximus himself is the one who there excuses himself; as also in other places where he seemed in some way to favour the new doctrine. Here he plainly shows how he called the single operation of God alone in the blessed deification: namely that the action which is blessedness (the vision and enjoyment of God) comes about in us with God working above the whole order of nature; although we do truly work, and vitally, but not as if we were ourselves the principle and authors of the action, but as drawn by God toward what is divine; in which very manner Maximus says that it is not a requital of the saints for just works, since it wholly exceeds the merits of works, which are themselves God's gifts in us, as Augustine says. But on these things the theologians.

text: Τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν πάσχουσαν. Quasi scilicet passive, divino quodam Dei experimento, et quo unus ipse agens videatur; veluti se res habet in principali agente motum imprimente, et in instrumento recipiente; cujus ipse motus instrumenti efficitur. Sic alte Maximus altum adeo pertractat θεώρημα, nec quidquam Christi mysterio officere ostendit: quod non ea motione ac afflatu illapsuque explicandum, sed quod Verbum vere homo factum est, ac quidquid hominis erat, una
anchorLine: τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν πάσχουσαν (k)· ἀλλὰ μόνην ὑπέδειξα
en: 'Experiencing the enjoyment of good things.' As if, that is, passively, through a certain divine experience of God, and in which God alone seems to be the agent; just as the case is with a principal agent imparting motion and an instrument receiving it, whose motion is brought about in the instrument. So Maximus deeply treats so lofty a theorem, and shows that it does nothing against the mystery of Christ: it is not to be explained by that motion, breath and inflow, but because the Word was truly made man, and whatever belonged to man, together ...

text: dempto peccato assumpserit. Turriano desunt una fere aut altera linea; nec quæ habet, ipsa illi satis expedita sunt. Quem ultimo scholio perstringit Nilum, Dufrenii codicis Antiquarius, idem sæpius sugillat quasi non ecclesiastice de Christo ejusque mysterio sentientem. Quis vero hic Nilus sit, ac num cujus exstat libellus adversus primatum papæ, Nilus Thessalonicensis, cui erudite respondit Matthæus Caryophilus archiepiscopus Iconiensis, vir egregie orthodoxus, incertum est. Si tamen is ipse est, et hoc observatu dignum, quod sic Romanæ infensus Ecclesiæ ac schismaticus, nec in exploratis dogmatis sanæ fidei est: videantque nostri novatores quem tanti hominem faciant, suæque velint aciei præstantem ducem.
anchorLine: (anchor on p-0023: τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν πάσχουσαν (k))
en: ... took on everything of man, sin excepted. Turrianus lacks about a line or two here; and what he has is not sufficiently worked out for him. The Nilus whom he touches in the last scholion, the Antiquary of Dufresne's codex, he often criticises as if he did not think ecclesiastically about Christ and his mystery. Who this Nilus is, and whether he is the Nilus of Thessalonica whose book against the primacy of the pope survives, to whom Matthew Caryophilus, archbishop of Iconium, a man outstandingly orthodox, replied learnedly, is uncertain. But if it is the same man, this too is worth noting: that though hostile to the Roman Church and a schismatic, he is not unsound in the examined points of sound faith; and let our innovators see what man they make of him, and whether they wish to have him as a leader at the head of their line.

text: Κεφάλ. ν΄. Sic Dufrenii codex breviate, quæ nota est capitis quinquagesimi, ejus operis, quod Maximus ad Marinum presbyterum scripsit; sicque ex Romanis codd. Caput quinquagesimum, rite ascripsit Lucas Holstenius. At Turriani codex, ipse forsitan quod et apographum a reverendissimo Gerasimo Blaccho acceptum, Κεφάλαια πεντήκοντα, dum reddit, Capita quinquaginta, parum certe accuratum agit interpretem, cui nec sic apertum mendum subolucrit. Quis enim Quinquaginta hic Capita vel somniet, non unum ipsum Quinquagesimum: a quo statim sequitur Quinquagesimum primum; quæ duo ex tanta illa Maximi lucubratione nobis exstant? Ad eumdem Marinum, Πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν Μαρῖνον, unius Blacchi codicis est. Quodque tantum Maximi opus ad Marinum excidit, cujus nulla dubitatio esse potest, una hac ac altera spica tanti manipuli in his quasi Collectaneis nobis superstite, quid mirum excidisse et epistolam, qua apud eumdem excusat pro diplomate Roma a papa misso Constantinopolim, ut nusquam integra exstet, sed sola quasi excerpta, iis passim relata, qui de Spiritus processione, tuenda aut impugnanda Latinorum hoc argumento fide, scripserunt, ut valde frivolum inde argumentum ducant etiam viri catholici, quasi περὶ νοθείας laborare intelligatur, cum alias Maximi characteres habeat, τῶν σχολαστικῶν, nec veterum, pro Maximi ætate, testimonio careat. Magis miror, quod card. Baronius opus hoc quinquaginta capitibus distinctum, ipsam existimat ad Marinum epistolam, quæ est hic prima inter editas Gretsero ex Turriani versione, cum illa vix excedat duodecim capita: post quam sequitur caput illud 51. ex dicto opere de operationibus et voluntatibus. Nimirum granditas operis prohibuit ill. scriptorem librum adire, alioquin plurimum de re ecclesiastica meritus esset, si nactus integrum ejusmodi opus, saltem indicasset.
anchorLine: Ἐκ τῆς περὶ ἐνεργειῶν καὶ θελημάτων πραγματείας, κεφάλ. ν΄ (l).
en: Chapter 50. So Dufresne's codex gives it in abbreviated form, which is the sign of the fiftieth chapter of that work which Maximus wrote to Marinus the priest; and so, from the Roman codices, Lucas Holstenius rightly wrote 'chapter fiftieth'. But Turrianus's codex (perhaps itself a copy received from the most reverend Gerasimus Blachus), in rendering κεφάλαια πεντήκοντα as 'fifty chapters', acts as a rather inaccurate interpreter, to whom even so the plain error did not occur. For who would imagine 'fifty chapters' here, not the fiftieth alone, which is immediately followed by the fifty-first, the two of that great labour of Maximus that survive for us? 'To the same Marinus' (Πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν Μαρῖνον) is found in one Blachus codex alone. And that so great a work of Maximus to Marinus has perished, about which there can be no doubt, with only this and one other ear of so great a sheaf surviving to us in these 'collectanea', what wonder that the letter too has perished in which he excuses himself to the same Marinus about the diploma sent from Rome by the pope to Constantinople, so that it exists nowhere entire but only as excerpts, reported here and there by those who wrote on the procession of the Spirit, defending or attacking the argument of the Latins, so that even Catholic men draw a quite frivolous argument from it, as if it were understood to be a question of spuriousness, when otherwise it has Maximus's scholastic characteristics, and is not lacking in the testimony of the ancients, given Maximus's date. I am more astonished that Cardinal Baronius thinks this work, distinguished by fifty chapters, to be the very letter to Marinus which stands here first among those edited by Gretser from Turrianus's version, though that scarcely exceeds twelve chapters; after which follows that chapter 51 from the said work on the operations and wills. Obviously the size of the work prevented the illustrious writer from consulting the book; otherwise he would have deserved very well of the church, had he found the work entire and at least pointed it out.

text: Ποιότητα. Sic quoque Turr. Qualitatem non divisam: sed palam mendum est, ac reponendum, quantitatem, quam aliis passim locis, distinctionis omnino comitem ait, ejusque notam numerum esse, qui ipse minime dividat; sed pro eorum quæ numerata sunt, ratione, vel continuus, vel discretus exsistat. Paulo etiam superius, nihil apte idem Turrianus, ita jungit, διασπίγγων τὴν σύγχυσιν τῶν ἐναντίων, confusionem contrariorum astringat; quasi Maximus contraria vocet naturas in Christo, aut qualitates; non ipsam distinctionem et confusionem; quibus contrariis Nestorius Severusque contraria statuebant, non evertebant, uti ipse Maximus satis clare exponit. Stulta religiositas sic scribæ festinantis manu in præceps agi, ut vel cum luce clarior aberratio est, ipseque perspicuus auctoris sensus, emendare nolis, ac vel indicare quod emendandum videris.
anchorLine: τῶν διαφερόντων ποιότητα (m), γινώσκων (read from page thumbnail; 600 dpi line not examined)
en: 'Quality.' So also Turrianus: 'quality not divided'; but the error is plain, and one must restore 'quantity', which in other places he says is always the companion of distinction, and its mark is number, which itself divides not at all, but according to the nature of the things numbered exists either continuous or discrete. A little earlier too, Turrianus joins something not at all aptly, 'confusion of contraries', as if Maximus called the contrary things natures in Christ, or qualities, not the very distinction and confusion; by which contraries Nestorius and Severus established opposites, they did not overturn them, as Maximus himself explains clearly enough. A foolish scrupulousness, thus to be carried headlong by the hand of a hurrying scribe, so that even where the error is clearer than daylight and the author's sense itself is evident, you would not emend, or at least point out what you see needs emending.

text: Συνήγαγε τῇ τῶν γνωμικῶν θελημάτων διαφορᾷ. Clara Maximi sententia; eo quod distinctæ voluntates ex sententia, sequi majoris ac minoris bonitatis esse, quod scilicet vicissim hoc illoque modo procedant, varientque boni prosecutione; a quo proinde nihil vetat deficere: quod est Christo demere τὸ ἀναμάρτητον, quod ab omni immunis peccato est. Turr. Et conjunxit cum differentia voluntatum ex sententia, differentiam sententiæ; eadem voce reddens, quod est Græce διαφορὰ καὶ παραλλαγή: quæ voces longe differunt, ac quarum Maximus pro maximo absurdo alteram infert ex altera in ejusmodi voluntatibus, id est, gnomicis; nempe ex distinctione contrarietatem, contra ac dicit Greg. Τὸ ἐκείνου θέλειν, οὐδὲν ὑπεναντίον Θεῷ, ac vertibilitatem in malum seu minus bonum, humanæ Christi voluntatis ex sententia, ut quæ non Verbi nutu regatur, ut personæ moventis atque utentis, sed ipsa suo.
anchorLine: (Greek column, near '... τῶν γνωμικῶν θελημάτων διαφορᾷ (n), καὶ τὴν τῆς γνώμης παραλλαγὴν'; read from page thumbnail, not at 600 dpi)
en: 'He brought together by the difference of the gnomic wills.' Maximus's meaning is clear: because distinct wills by judgment follow a greater or lesser goodness, namely, that they proceed now in this way, now in that, and differ in the pursuit of the good; whence nothing prevents their falling away from it: which is to take from Christ the 'sinless', which means that he is immune from all sin. Turrianus: 'And he joined with the difference of the wills by judgment the difference of judgment', rendering both with the same word, which in Greek is διαφορά and παραλλαγή: words which differ widely, and of which Maximus, as the greatest absurdity, infers the one from the other in wills of this kind, that is, gnomic ones; namely contrariety from distinction, contrary to what Gregory says: 'His willing is nothing opposed to God'; and (infers) changeability toward evil or lesser good in the human will of Christ by judgment, as one that is not governed by the nod of the Word, as of the person moving and using it, but by its own.
